raw.assessment: Full assembly gives workers an opportunity to encounter insertion problems and check an order before dispatch, but its benefit is unmeasured. The 11-minute median exceeds the time target; seven of ten customers achieved their arrangement unaided. Five partition complaints suggest a contents problem without establishing a verified defect rate. Mixed batches contain every extreme delay, while repeated three-compartment orders take seven to nine minutes: this limiting observation suggests the incumbent sometimes approaches the target, but layout complexity and switching are confounded. Overlapping partition widths also limit a width-only explanation of reinsertion. Neither sequence effects nor fit causes are established.

openings.claim: Switching between order configurations may contribute to selection and checking delays beyond the work required by compartment count.
openings.delta: Separates a potentially changeable sequencing cost from inherent assembly complexity.
openings.prediction: For identical layout and color workloads, blocked sequences reduce selection/checking time relative to alternating sequences, even within the same compartment count.
openings.probe: Use reusable sample orders with both workers and identical contents in blocked and alternating sequences, counterbalancing sequence order. Record selection, insertion, checking and packing separately, plus contents errors. Keep accepted orders and dispatch timing unchanged; limit rehearsal to available working time.
assumptions: Rehearsal time is available before the fixed deadline.
Samples can be reused without material wear dominating results.

openings.claim: Does uncertainty about short-partition placement persist when contents and insertion feasibility are verified, and does an order-specific diagram reduce it?
openings.delta: Distinguishes information ambiguity from missing, incorrect or mechanically unusable parts.
openings.prediction: If diagram ambiguity contributes, customers receiving an order-specific diagram ask fewer placement questions and more often finish unaided despite equivalent verified parts.
openings.probe: Assign five of the ten willing participants to the current diagram and five to a hand-drawn order-specific diagram, using matched layouts and verified reusable samples. Record unaided completion within ten minutes, placement questions and insertion failures. Treat results as exploratory; price production diagrams before adoption against both cost limits.
assumptions: Sample verification does not itself reveal placement to participants.
Any production change must also fit workshop time and cost limits.

raw.assessment: One linked mechanism hypothesis merits a bounded sample test. Combined timing, reported missing parts and insertion retries do not establish their causes or prove that removing workshop assembly will help.

openings.claim: Hypothesis: full workshop assembly creates demand for insertion retries and arrangement checking. In a counterfactual forbidding workshop preassembly, supply an order-specific partition kit on a compartment-count checklist whose part silhouettes and orientation marks also form the customer assembly map. Preserve the existing base, partition geometry, selected count and exterior color. Hybrid parents are physical completeness checking and layout-specific instruction; their interaction makes the checked inventory itself the assembly interface.
openings.delta: Change the workshop/customer relationship from delivering a completed arrangement to delivering a verified arrangement kit. Remove the dependency on workshop insertion as the verification interface. Its former obligations are complete and correct inventory, fit verification, correct arrangement, retention during transport and protection. Replace them with order-to-parts matching, silhouette/count checking, sampled insertion-fit checks, a map for the exact ordered layout, and secured protective packing. Replacement dependencies also include legible orientation cues, accurate map preparation, customer insertion ability, available packing materials and an affordable preparation process. Sample checks may fail to replace unit-level fit verification.
openings.prediction: If preassembly generates avoidable work, removing it reduces total workshop time even after kit checking and packing are counted; customer short-partition placement errors need not increase with an exact-layout map. Increased customer failures or replacement checking time would contradict the proposed benefit.
openings.probe: Use the 15 sample allowance across all three compartment counts to compare matched assembled and kit workflows, timing selection, insertion, verification, map preparation and packing separately. Have ten participants try an assigned workflow unaided; record completeness, arrangement errors and insertion difficulty. Inspect transport retention, footprint and assortment capacity. Cost preparation and recurring materials and check delivery feasibility before any pilot change. Samples screen feasibility; the 60-unit pilot must independently meet the stated success measures.
assumptions: Maps and packing can be prepared within 500 initial and 0.40 recurring units and the fixed delivery date.
Existing reversible slots remain usable by customers.
Kit protection and alternative checks can fulfill the former assembly obligations without increasing missing or incorrect parts.

critiques.assumption: An order-specific map can independently establish both inventory correctness and the intended arrangement when it also supplies the checking template.
critiques.limitation: A mistaken map could agree perfectly with a mistaken kit. Silhouette checking would then establish internal consistency while dispatching the wrong ordered arrangement. D2-O3 supports investigating contents errors, but supplies no evidence that this common-source failure occurred.
critiques.opening: Keep the shared inventory/assembly surface, but derive its acceptance check directly from the original order slip and existing cutting templates.
critiques.comparison: Physical completeness checking alone counts what its template expects; layout instruction alone guides placement. A1 combines these benefits through one surface, but also couples their errors. An independent order-to-template check could retain that interaction while detecting shared specification mistakes. It fails if the second check merely copies the map, if the original order is wrong, or if checking consumes the time saving.
critiques.probe: Challenge reusable sample kits with known, deliberately introduced map/parts discrepancies and self-consistent wrong map/kit pairs; compare detection with and without direct order-slip checking. These are proposed tests, not observed failures.

openings.claim: Hypothesis: independently validating each layout map against its order before using that map for kit checking prevents a shared map error from becoming an undetected packing error.
openings.delta: Adds an independent source of correctness to A1 rather than another check against the same possibly mistaken representation.
openings.prediction: Direct order-derived checks detect more self-consistent wrong kits than map-only checks, while correct kits remain straightforward for customers to assemble.
openings.probe: Within the 15-sample allowance, use balanced correct and seeded-error kits across compartment counts and colors; counterbalance worker/check order and conceal seeded status. Record detection, false alarms, and total preparation/checking/packing time. Correct every seeded kit before ten participants test the resulting maps unaided. Separately retain A1 fit and transport probes. Price added work/materials before adoption; these samples cannot establish the 60-order success thresholds.
assumptions: Original order slips accurately encode accepted choices.
Independent checking fits available working time, the fixed delivery date, and both cost limits.
Footprint, capacity, reversible partitions, selected counts and colors remain unchanged.

openings.claim: Configuration switching may add selection/checking delays.
openings.probe: Counterbalance blocked/alternating reusable orders for both workers; time stages and errors.
openings.uncertainty: Complexity confounds existing timing; rehearsal time and wear matter.

openings.claim: Exact-layout diagrams may resolve short-partition ambiguity independently of contents or fit.
openings.discriminator: Fewer questions with equally verified parts.
openings.probe: Assign five participants per diagram, match layouts; record ten-minute unaided completion and insertion failures.
openings.uncertainty: Small exploratory groups; familiarity and verification cues may bias results.

openings.claim: Replace workshop preassembly with an order-specific kit whose checked silhouettes/orientation map guide assembly.
openings.discriminator: Total workshop savings survive preparation/checking/packing without more customer failures.
openings.probe: Use 15 samples across counts; compare assembled/kit stages, completeness, customer placement, fit and transport protection.
openings.uncertainty: Transfers insertion to customers; sampled fit may miss unit defects. Retry causes remain unknown; widths overlap.

openings.claim: Independently check maps against orders/templates to catch shared map/kit mistakes.
openings.discriminator: Detect self-consistent wrong kits beyond map-only checking.
openings.probe: Within sample allowance, conceal balanced seeded errors across counts/colors; counterbalance checks, measure detection/false alarms/time; correct before customer use.
openings.uncertainty: Failure is conjectural; incorrect orders, copied checks or extra work defeat benefit.

post_distill.decision: Screen within shared resources; retain 30x20 footprint, capacity, reversible slots, accepted counts/colors and deadline. Price <=500 initial and <=0.40/order. Complaints are unverified; samples cannot establish pilot targets: >=59/60 complete, median <=8 minutes, >=90% unaided.
